title: How an if becomes a jump
objective: By the end of this lesson you can map any C conditional onto its compiled form, read a conditional jump's condition correctly, and explain why an unsigned comparison can replace two range checks.

blocks.text: There are no if statements in machine code. Every conditional in every program reduces to the same two-step pattern: an instruction that sets the flags, and an instruction that reads them.

blocks.caption: Three instructions read the flags, and they differ only in what they do next
lines: cmp  edi, esi          ; set the flags from edi - esi
jl   .Lsomewhere       ; JUMP if the condition holds
setl al                ; SET a byte to 1 if the condition holds
cmovl eax, edx         ; COPY only if the condition holds
/* Same condition, three ways of acting on it. The suffix is identical
across all three families, so learning the conditions once covers
every conditional instruction in the architecture. */

rows: if (a == b) X
cmp a,b ; jne skip ; X ; skip:
if (a != b) X
cmp a,b ; je skip ; X ; skip:
if (a < b) X  (signed)
cmp a,b ; jge skip ; X ; skip:
if (a < b) X  (unsigned)
cmp a,b ; jae skip ; X ; skip:
if (p) X
test p,p ; je skip ; X ; skip:
if (x & MASK) X
test x,MASK ; je skip ; X ; skip:

blocks.title: The condition is inverted
blocks.text: Notice that if (a == b) compiles to jump-if-NOT-equal. The compiler emits code that skips the body, so the jump tests the opposite of the source condition. This trips up almost everyone reading disassembly for the first time: when you see jne, the source almost certainly said ==. Read a conditional jump as 'skip the following block when...' rather than as the condition itself.
When there is no jump at all

blocks.caption: Real output for a three-way comparison
lines: int classify(int x) { if (x < 0) return -1; if (x == 0) return 0; return 1; }
_classify:
test  edi, edi
sets  al          ; al = 1 if x is negative
setg  cl          ; cl = 1 if x is greater than zero
movsx eax, cl
ret
/* Two ifs in the source, no jumps in the output. One test set the flags,
two set instructions asked two different questions of them, and a
subtraction combined the answers. */

blocks.text: An if in the source is not evidence of a branch in the binary. This function has two conditionals and zero jumps: the compiler used the set family instead, turning the conditions into 0-or-1 values and doing arithmetic on them. When a profiler shows no branch mispredictions in a function full of ifs, this is usually why.
A switch, and the trick inside it

blocks.caption: Eight cases compiled at -O1
lines: A switch over 0..7 returning 71, 3, 42, 8, 99, 17, 4, 55:
_jt:
mov  eax, -1                          ; the default
cmp  edi, 7
ja   .Ldone                           ; UNSIGNED above -- see below
mov  eax, edi
lea  rcx, [rip + switch.table.jt]
mov  eax, dword ptr [rcx + 4*rax]     ; read the answer from a table
.Ldone:
ret
switch.table.jt:  .long 71, 3, 42, 8, 99, 17, 4, 55
/* Eight cases became one bounds check and one table load. Note ja, the
UNSIGNED above: a negative x read as unsigned is an enormous number,
so a single unsigned comparison rejects both x < 0 and x > 7. One
instruction doing the work of two range checks. */

blocks.title: One unsigned comparison replaces two signed ones
blocks.text: Checking 0 <= x && x <= 7 normally takes two comparisons. Reading x as unsigned collapses them into one: any negative value becomes a number above two billion, so a single 'above 7' test rejects it along with everything genuinely too large. This idiom appears in almost every bounds check in optimised code — and recognising it matters, because when it is written incorrectly it is exactly how a negative index gets past a length check.

rows: Few cases
A chain of cmp and je
Dense range, arbitrary results
A bounds check and a table lookup
Dense range, arbitrary code
A bounds check and an indirect jump through a table of addresses
Dense range, results in arithmetic progression
Arithmetic — no table and no branch at all
Sparse values
A chain of comparisons, or a binary search over the values

blocks.text: The fourth row is real: a switch returning 10, 20, 30 up to 80 for inputs 0 to 7 compiles to two lea instructions and a cmov, because the compiler noticed the results were 10x + 10. A switch is a request, not an instruction, and what it becomes depends entirely on the shape of the values in it.

blocks.title: An indirect jump is where static reading gets hard
blocks.text: jmp rax or jmp qword ptr [rcx + 8*rax] transfers control somewhere the disassembler cannot determine without knowing the register's value. Jump tables, function pointers, virtual method calls and dynamic dispatch all produce these. When a disassembly seems to end abruptly, look for an indirect jump — the code continues, but only the runtime knows where. This is the point at which static analysis usually needs a debugger's help, which is what the tooling module is about.

blocks.title: Map source to jumps
steps: Write six small functions, one for each row of the first table, and compile at -O1
Confirm each conditional jump tests the opposite of the source condition
Write the three-way classify function and confirm it compiles without a jump
Write a switch with eight consecutive cases returning unrelated values and find the table
Change the returned values to 10, 20, 30 and so on, and watch the table disappear
Write a switch with cases 1, 100 and 5000 and see what replaces the table
Find the unsigned bounds-check idiom in one of your compilations
Explain in one sentence why it rejects negative inputs
blocks.expected: Inverted jump conditions throughout, a branchless classify, a lookup table that vanishes when the results become an arithmetic progression, and comparison chains for sparse cases. The sparse case is worth noticing: with only three widely separated values there is nothing to index, so the compiler falls back to comparing — the same decision you would make by hand.

cheatsheet: Every conditional is two steps: set the flags, then read them
jcc jumps, setcc sets a byte to 0 or 1, cmovcc copies — all use the same condition names
Compiled conditions are inverted: if (a == b) becomes jne past the body
Read a conditional jump as 'skip the block when...', not as the source condition
test p, p is the compiled form of if (p)
test x, MASK is the compiled form of if (x & MASK)
An if in the source does not imply a branch in the binary; setcc may replace it
cmp x, 7 followed by ja is an unsigned bounds check rejecting negatives too
A switch may become a comparison chain, a table lookup, an indirect jump, or arithmetic
An indirect jump is where static reading stops and a debugger becomes necessary

checkpoint.prompt: You see cmp edi, esi followed by a forward jne. What did the source most likely say?
checkpoint.explanation: The compiler jumps past the body when the source condition fails, so the jump tests the opposite. Read a conditional jump as 'skip the following block when...'. Almost every compiled if has this inversion.

checkpoint.prompt: A function with two if statements compiles to setCC instructions (sets, setg), a sub, and no jumps. What happened?

choices.A: The optimiser inlined a branch predictor
choices.C: The conditions moved into a called function

checkpoint.explanation: Each condition became a 0-or-1 byte, and arithmetic combined them into the result (x>0) - (x<0) gives 1, 0 or -1. An if in the source is not evidence of a branch in the binary.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does cmp edi, 7 followed by ja correctly reject negative values as well as values above 7?

choices.B: It does not; that is a bug
choices.D: The compiler adds a separate check

checkpoint.explanation: A negative value read as unsigned is an enormous number, so it is above 7 too. One unsigned comparison replaces two signed ones. It appears in nearly every optimised bounds check — and getting it wrong is how a negative index passes a length test.

checkpoint.prompt: A switch over eight consecutive cases compiles to two lea instructions and a cmov, with no table. Why?

choices.A: The case results formed an arithmetic progression
choices.B: The switch was on an enum, which never uses tables
choices.C: Eight cases is below the table threshold
choices.D: The compiler ran out of memory for the table

checkpoint.explanation: The compiler computed them instead of storing them. A switch is a request, not an instruction. Returning 10, 20 up to 80 for inputs 0 to 7 is just 10x + 10, so no table or branch is needed.
